tier_reason: Upgraded B->A. mold README benchmark gives lld vs wild vs mold wall-clock times, and the machines are named (Threadripper 7980X / Ubuntu 24.04, M1 Ultra / Fedora Asahi 42). It also gives the build/benchmark configuration (all linkers built from source in release configuration as of 2026-08-28, default options, median of 3 runs after warm-up), and the benchmark code is public: the Zenodo record 21882261 (bench.tar.gz) includes the build and evaluation scripts plus all linker inputs. Tier rules say who ran it does not matter, so the rival-README cap to B does not apply.

corrections.claimed_speedup: In mold's README benchmark table (linkers built 2026-08-28, median of 3 runs), wild links faster than lld on every row where wild can link (7 programs per table x 4 tables = 28 rows). Examples on the Threadripper 7980X, debug builds: Blender 4.72s(lld)->1.98s(wild)=2.4x, ClickHouse 6.62s->4.40s=1.5x, Godot 1.77s->1.08s=1.6x, Chromium 16.64s->3.98s=4.2x. Across the 28 supported rows, lld/wild runs from 1.38x to 4.18x, median ~2.1x (derived from page data). The same page shows wild slower than mold (mold claims 1.9x faster than wild at the median). wild's own BENCHMARKING.md hyperfine output (ripgrep: wild 10.88x faster than GNU ld, 1.67x faster than mold) is explicitly an illustrative example ('with different values'), not a reported result.
corrections.workload: mold README benchmark: 9 programs (Blender 5.2, Chromium 145, Clang 21, ClickHouse 26.1, Firefox 149, Godot 4.6, LibreOffice 26.2, PyTorch 2.9, TensorFlow 2.21, plus ARM64 builds of Chromium and Firefox) linked in debug and release configurations on an AMD Ryzen Threadripper 7980X and an Apple M1 Ultra (perf cores only). Times are wall-clock medians of 3 runs after a warm-up. Per the page, wild's N/A rows mean wild cannot link that program (TensorFlow, Firefox debug, ARM64 Chromium/Firefox). Chromium release rows are N/A for a different reason: wild does not implement --icf=all.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: All three linkers (lld, wild, mold) were built from source in release configuration as of 2026-08-28 and run with their default options. The toolchain/compiler versions used to build the linkers are not stated.
corrections.caveats: The primary benchmark is in the README of a rival project (mold, whose author competes with wild). That page shows wild beating lld on every supported row but losing to mold on most rows. wild cannot link several programs in the suite (TensorFlow, Firefox debug, ARM64 Chromium/Firefox) and lacks --icf=all. wild also publishes its own benchmarks: benchmarks/ryzen-9955hx.md (AMD Ryzen 9 9955HX, runner code in benchmarks/runner, config in ryzen-9955hx.toml) compares against LLD 21.1.8, mold and GNU ld, but its numbers exist only as SVG charts (e.g. the clang-release chart labels LLD 21.1.8 as +400% vs Wild 0.10.0). BENCHMARKING.md shows only example output. The repository was transferred from davidlattimore/wild to the wild-linker org, and the old URL redirects. GitHub reports the license as Apache-2.0 only, but the README and the LICENSE-APACHE/LICENSE-MIT files confirm a dual license.

notes: Numbers verified against the mold README table; the record's claim that wild is faster on 'most rows' is corrected to 'every supported row'. The record's workload wrongly said TensorFlow/Firefox N/A was due to missing ICF: the page says those are programs wild cannot link. Metadata matches (3,998 stars, last commit 2026-09-24, not archived, not a fork). The record said wild had no numbers of its own; that is wrong, since wild's in-repo benchmarks/ directory has them.

tier_reason: First-party misc/benchmarks.md gives stock ld vs zld times for Signal, XUL and Storage.framework, with the full ld command lines. The hardware is vague ('high-end mac desktop', '2014 macbook pro'), and there is no run count, variance or benchmark harness, so these are first-party numbers short of A.

corrections.is_fork_of: Apple ld64 (open-source release; README says 'This project is a fork of the Apple linker, ld'; not a GitHub fork)

notes: All numbers match benchmarks.md exactly: 390->250ms, 5.2s->2.20s, 495->340ms; 2014 MBP 790->540, 10.3s->5.4s, 940->625. The '40% faster' is the README's 'file an issue if ... not at least 40% faster'. Repo is archived (MIT, 1,191 stars, last commit 2023-02-15), so the abandoned status is correct. The only change is is_fork_of, because the README calls zld a fork of Apple's ld.

tier_reason: This is a peer-reviewed PLDI'19 paper. Figure 8 compares staged combinators vs ocamlyacc/ocamllex, the paper states the compiler (BER MetaOCaml N107) and hardware (AMD FX 8320, 16GB, Debian, Core_bench, 95% CIs), and the benchmark code is public (benchmarks/ + Makefile 'make bench'). Compiler flags are not stated in the paper, so it falls short of A.
notes: Figure 8 values match: staged/ocamlyacc arith 14.31/10.96, pgn 33.26/21.29, ppm 11.83/6.75, sexp 43.65/28.6, json 60.32/80.42 (MB/s). The paper text states 'except JSON' and '75% for PPM'. The repo Makefile builds the benchmarks with default ocamlopt flags via ocamlbuild, and the current README targets the 4.11.1+BER switch rather than the paper's N107. Metadata is correct: MIT, 105 stars, last commit 2025-05-16, stale.

tier_reason: These are first-party numbers from the project's own harness (tests/bench.py). Compiler, flags and protobuf version are stated (g++-13 / clang++-20, -O3 -DNDEBUG, protobuf 4.25.3), but no CPU model appears in docs/benchmarks.md, architecture.md or the README. It is not a peer-reviewed or independent third-party suite either, so it is C, not B.

corrections.caveats: The CPU model is not stated anywhere in the benchmark docs (only a 'quiesced box' with SMT/turbo off and core pinning), so this falls short of A. The numbers are first-party and come from a very new, low-star project. Per the doc, part of the arena-vs-protoc gap is a feature gap: protoc validates UTF-8 on every proto3 string and RapidProto does not, and RapidProto borrows strings/bytes as views into the input instead of copying them. The streaming decoder is slower than protozero on large packed arrays. The authors call the ratios 'a box-specific rule of thumb, not a cross-machine constant'.

notes: All claimed figures appear on docs/benchmarks.md: ~7x arena vs protoc+Arena on g++-13 (~6x clang), 0.49x payload memory, streaming ~12x vs protoc+Arena and ~1.8x vs protozero, OSM PBF protobuf-layer +61% (arena warm, 441 vs 274 MB/s). Metadata is correct: Apache-2.0, 3 stars, created 2026-06-28, last commit 2026-09-14. The only change is the tier, B->C.

tier_reason: The benchmark is first-party: the zserio-protobuf-benchmarks repo is by the same NDS org, has 6 stars and is not peer-reviewed. The code (scripts/benchmark.sh), compiler (gcc 11.3.0) and CPU (i7-9850H) are public or stated, but optimization flags are not stated on the page; the scripts only default to a CMake Release build. That makes it C, not B.

corrections.workload: For each of 4 schemas (addressbook, Protobuf's own documentation example; apollo; carsales; simpletrace), the harness loads the JSON dataset and serializes it to binary as untimed setup. It then times only deserialization of that blob: protobuf ParseFromString in a loop (100 iterations by default), and zserio's read in the same way. The reported Time is per decode. C++, gcc 11.3.0, Protobuf 3.21.12 vs Zserio 2.10, on an Intel i7-9850H under Linux Mint 21.1.
corrections.claimed_speedup: Zserio-generated C++ decodes faster than protoc-generated C++ (ParseFromString) on all 4 datasets: addressbook 1.478ms vs 1.731ms (~1.17x), apollo 0.244ms vs 0.641ms (~2.63x), carsales 1.374ms vs 2.053ms (~1.49x), simpletrace 0.221ms vs 0.386ms (~1.75x). The byte-aligned schema variants are faster still: addressbook_align 0.844ms (~2.05x) and carsales_align 0.925ms (~2.22x) (derived from page data).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: gcc 11.3.0. Optimization flags are not stated on the page; the benchmark scripts default to a CMake Release build (scripts/common_tools.sh).
corrections.caveats: The timed operation is deserialization only (protobuf ParseFromString vs zserio read of a pre-serialized blob), not a JSON->binary->JSON round trip. The README calls itself 'an independent benchmark', but it is run and published by the same organization (Navigation Data Standard e.V.) that builds Zserio. The companion repo was last committed 2025-02-03 and compares old versions (Zserio 2.10, Protobuf 3.21.12). Zserio encodes no field IDs or lengths, trading protobuf's schema-evolution compatibility for size and speed. Speedups are modest (1.17x-2.63x). The zserio repo is BSD-3-Clause plus a note on the licensing of generated code, which is why GitHub reports NOASSERTION.

notes: The numbers match the zserio-protobuf-benchmarks README exactly. The record's 'round-trip' description was wrong: benchmark.sh times only ParseFromString, with JSON load and serialize outside the timer. The zserio repo's own benchmarks/README shows identical zserio C++ times but labels them Zserio 3.12 / gcc 11.4.0, a version inconsistency across the org's pages. Metadata is correct: BSD-3-Clause, 153 stars, last commit 2026-09-17, active.
